items.content:
Weekend hack: HackerTube. I was annoyed with YouTube's recommendations so I had Claude filter down 43M comments over 20 years of HN to 6,454 videos that keep being recommended. *Significantly* better viewing experience, ~2 hours with Opus 5.5:
https://t.co/JIhXN7OSh1

- Excellent recs without any logins (state is kept in local browser session)
- Thumbnail is a representative frame from middle of the video instead of the super duper A/B test hyper-optimized user uploads
- Underlying data from the comment analysis as one zip file, point your Claude at it and ask for your own version
- HackerTube Longs ✊

A bit more on the process:
I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac), Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I only talk to Claude and have it do everything, the only "manual work" I helped with in tandem was in the browser (reminiscent of MenuGen): 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box for serving and 3) I bought the domain name. Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, secure, harden, deploy and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing.

Many awesome projects that would have normally taken weeks/months even can now be few-shotted for breakfast. What else are we not thinking of.

items.content:
We’ve trained Claude to flag potential misuse in conversations, a technique we call self-assessment. Right after it responds, Claude gives a preliminary safety assessment of the conversation. 

Since we began using self-assessment in June, it has surfaced misuse that our other safeguards weren’t designed to catch. 

Because Claude has already read the conversation, self-assessment is very efficient. And unlike classifiers, which target a discrete set of harms, it draws on Claude’s own judgment, so it gets more accurate as our models improve.

Read more on our new Safeguards blog:
https://t.co/18j6zdHub4

New Anthropic research: progress on provable inference for large language models.

Here, we introduce FlashProve. Building on established cryptographic techniques, FlashProve allows developers to verify whether a given response came from a given AI model. It’s substantially more efficient than prior open-source methods for doing so. 

These proofs have a range of applications. They can, for instance, make it harder for attackers to hijack a chat, or enable safety evaluators to verify that the model they’re testing is the same one being served to customers.

For our full write-up, see here: https://t.co/OIZWPb6QZa

Further progress in provable inference will likely be an important part of improving trust in AI deployment. To that end, we're open-sourcing FlashProve’s code, here: https://t.co/7ky3Ir8V06

We’re grateful to our collaborators: Alessandro Chiesa, @GiacomoFenzi, @gwberg95, @miranda__christ, Rahul Dalal (https://t.co/pjWKLHWXyz) and Ben Mayer (@transmissions11).

Red-teaming is a vital part of model safety t
items.content:
New Anthropic research: Automating subtle emergent misalignment research.

Red-teaming is a vital part of model safety testing, but it’s also limited by researchers’ time. To see if we could automate it, we set thousands of Claude agents the task of evading a training data monitor.

These agents developed training data that looked harmless to monitors (like a veteran wrestler mentoring a newcomer, or a Q&A about professional beekeeping), but that in fact taught misaligned behavior.

Examples like these can be used to directly improve future training data monitors. This research is only a first step, but it suggests that future red-teaming efforts could improve much further, using better models and more compute.

Read the full post on the Alignment Science Blog: https://t.co/24Gs1oSw7Q

items.title: We’re sharing how our biology research team worked with Claude to map the first 3D structure of a vault particle from ba
items.content:
We’re sharing how our biology research team worked with Claude to map the first 3D structure of a vault particle from bacterial life.

Vault particles are a longstanding mystery. They are barrel-shaped objects, among the largest protein structures found in our cells. They were first discovered by Leonard Rome and Nancy Kedersha in 1986, but their function remains unknown.

With Claude, we’ve found results that might bring us closer to solving that mystery.

Until now, vaults were only known in the cells of complex things like animals and plants. We have shown that similar proteins from bacteria (and the viruses that infect them) can also assemble into vaults. Finding the structures in these simpler forms of life may make it easier to investigate their function in our own cells.

For our life sciences team, the project was also a demonstration of the potential (and the limitations) of using AI to accelerate science.

In our full piece, we discuss how Claude was able to dramatically speed up some stages—manually determining the vault particle’s structure would have taken weeks to months of painstaking work, but here it took days. We also discuss how Claude made some simple mistakes along the way, and how we collaborated with our machine learning researchers to address them.

Read more: https://t.co/KowVVCSPp8

items.content:
There are a few notable counter-examples (e.g. HAL) but this is basically right for a lot of pre-2000 sci-fi.

I think getting AI right from e.g. somewhere in the ~1970s would require a fairly complicated set of inferences, probably the biggest things would be:

Image the world in 50 years.
1. "Digital knowledge work / computing". The vast majority of knowledge work (which makes up a very large fraction of the economy) goes digital. As computers get cheaper, much of society’s work happens on screens, over billions of machines in homes and offices.
2. "Internet". Similar to ARPANET (and see Licklider’s “Intergalactic Computer Network” (1963)), this creates demand for a global network of computers where people work, argue, teach, joke, and socialize.
3. "Big data". This creates a very large, compounding repository of digital information, with traces of how people reason, how they create, what they know etc.
4. "Statistical learning". Trying to program intelligence by hand is extremely difficult. But Shannon's n-gram approximations of English (1948) show examples of how language has statistical structure that can be "learned". You could imagine doing so over extensions of cybernetic computing (e.g. in the style of Rosenblatt's Perceptron 1958). So instead of programming thought, we could fit a statistical model to the record.
5. "LLMs". This might lead to something along the lines of ELIZA (1966), but with enough data (per 1-3), and enough compute (see Moore's law 1965), the imitation might become of extreme hight fidelity to the point that it's economically extremely useful.
6. "Scaling laws". These networks may demand a huge amount of data / computing resources and expertise to train. It's plausible that the more of each you have, the better your ELIZA gets. The economics concentrate, where a few organizations build a few minds and then deploy copies of them digitally.

Something like that. Basically, it's a lot of leaps. You have to start with computers, to internet, to big data, to big compute (Moore's law), which then allow large-scale statistical learning approach based on neural networks, and then posit scaling laws, and then imagine the form factor of language models as a lot more sophisticated ELIZA. And you'd have to short everything else, most predominantly I think the idea that we'd figure out how to program robots by hand.

items.title: a16z's Martin Casado on the four mindsets people bring to investing, and why knowing yours stops you from justifying you
items.content:
a16z's Martin Casado on the four mindsets people bring to investing, and why knowing yours stops you from justifying your own bias:

1. Financial

"The correct proxy for the health of a business is the market it's going into and its finances. That's what it is. What are the SaaS metrics? What is the size of the market? That is a proxy for the entire business."

2. Productive

"You believe you're investing in a productive asset, and the productive asset is what's creating value. If you believe in that, as it creates value, it will create market... The type of diligence you do if you're a productive investor is more like, what is the technical approach? What are the adjacent markets?"

3. Frontier

"I think this is the romantic, idealized version of VC from the 60s and 70s, which is kind of YOLO. It's like, founders know better than VCs, and they've seen something that I don't see, and they're gonna go out there and do it. And, like, who am I to second guess them?"

4. Speculative

"It is always so surprising how prevalent it is... They don't even care about the asset. They just want to time a market, right?... They're like, 'Well, this looks cheap. It's clearly gonna go up in value' or, 'This is the top of the market, like, I'm gonna get out.'"

"...You can justify any deal or not justify any deal. So if you don't know what your beliefs are, you'll always basically just kind of justify whatever personal bias you have."

@martin_casado w/ @patrick_oshag on @InvestLikeBest

items.title: Ask HN: What's your current AI agentic setup?
items.content:
Ask HN: What's your current AI agentic setup? I'm curious how people on HN are using AI day to day, and came up with a list of questions I thought could be interesting to know. No need to answer every question of course, just wanted to get a gut feel how people are using AI.

1) What AI subscriptions are you personally paying for? (Claude, ChatGPT/Codex, Cursor, etc)

- Which tiers?

- Have you purchased multiple subscriptions from the same provider (eg two Claude accounts)?

2) Are you using models outside (or instead) of those subscriptions? For example, pay-as-you-go APIs, OpenRouter, or locally hosted models.

- Which models and providers?

3) What coding harnesses and interfaces are you using? Are you sticking with the default CLIs or IDE integrations, or using alternatives like OpenCode, Pi, Aider, Muse Code, or custom-built harnesses?

- What made you switch harnesses (if you switched)?

4) Are you using any agent orchestration or swarm tools?

- For example, Munder Difflin, Gas Town, Ruflo, or something custom.

5) Are you using broader agent platforms like OpenClaw / Hermes Agent / Grok bot / Dots / Muse?

- If you are using them, what are your main use cases?

-----

I know my workflow has differed significantly from a year ago, and so it would be interesting to capture a snapshot today of what people are using and why.

items.title: Tell HN: Gemini trains on chat history, even for subscribers (personal accounts)
items.content:
Tell HN: Gemini trains on chat history, even for subscribers (personal accounts) If you have a personal Google AI subscription, all your saved chat history in Gemini can be used for training and there is no way to opt out unless you turn off chat history or use temporary chat sessions. These chat transcripts may even be read by human reviewers. Although Google claims to disconnect them from your account when human-reviewed, they explicitly warn not to enter confidential information.

https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/16836988

“[Gemini app activity] is used to improve Google services for everyone, including by training generative AI models, if your Keep Activity setting is on.“

https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/13594961?hl=en#human_review

“A subset of chats are reviewed by human reviewers”

https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/13594961?hl=en#pn_retain_data

“Chats reviewed by human reviewers [...] are not deleted when you delete your activity. Instead, they are retained for up to three years.”

https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/13594961?hl=en#pn_data_usage

“Please don’t enter confidential information that you wouldn’t want a reviewer to see or Google to use to improve our services, including machine-learning technologies.”

To disable their training on your chat sessions, you need to turn off “Keep Activity” in Gemini’s settings. Turning that off means you’ll lose any chat sessions after 72 hours.

I learned this too late, thinking that having a paid subscription = not being turned into the product. Apparently paying is not enough.

Thank you to this user on HN for mentioning in another thread: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50355424

items.content:
Great way to think of your next AI use case ⬇️

You ended your work day and you still have items on your to-do list.

Read that list. 

Those are the the problems that AI is still not good enough to solve for, we can't or don't trust it enough to solve for, or may never be good enough to solve for.

"I have to review this email before I send it" - consider that you don't trust AI enough to reason on that issue or it still doesn't quite write like you. Perhaps spend more time on your "write like me" skill or build out another eval for that process to catch the most common or obvious things you're reviewing for. 

"I have to fill this thing out online and it has to be perfect" - then computer use isn't good enough, or you don't know it's good enough. If it makes sense, ask AI to complete the task one-by-one, watch it work, witness its performance. What, if anything, failed? Can you improve it for next time?

"I have to wait for Bobby to respond to my email" - consider additional workflows supporting on team alignment or team handoffs, something that nearly every enterprise I speak with is still struggling with.

Literally just end your work day and look at what is still left. 

That list will tell you what of your own workflows to improve with AI or where you can carve out a business for others with the same lingering list item.

items.title: Launch HN: Kino AI (YC S23) – AI media manager and video editor
items.content:
Launch HN: Kino AI (YC S23) – AI media manager and video editor Hi HN! I'm Luke from Kino (https://kino.ai). Kino lets you make great videos with your agents and your teammates. Storage of footage and assets, a rich video editor, and review links for teammates are all bundled into one. Your colleagues and Codex / Claude Code can work on the same timeline with review notes and footage all in one place. See a basic overview at https://kino.ai/walkthrough-video and our launch video (made entirely with Kino!) at https://kino.ai/launch-video

Opus 5.5 can edit videos and make great motion graphics now. But with a raw agent harness, you need to describe tiny edits either in words or in quick one-off UIs, you can’t refer to footage shared across your devices, and feedback from teammates comes as screenshots on Slack.

Kino is code-first. All editing, all motion graphics, all dragging of timeline items around, all teammate comments, and all 3D scenes are expressed as code, built on Remotion. This was hard to get right, as we found ourselves building a what-you-see-is-what-you-get editor for React, which we then turned into a video editor. For our launch video I told Claude-with-Kino to find a macOS Leopard install disk and reskin our whole video to match.

Kino is also fully collaborative and real-time, so you can see your teammates' cursors and exactly which part of the timeline they’re currently watching. For our launch video I had 5+ agents editing the timeline concurrently while my friend Donald had his swarm working a few minutes further down. Donald had one agent rotoscoping to make our visual effects work, I had an LLM color grading all media via our LUT support, and we both made tiny tweaks to the timeline along the way.

To make this code-first editor work with video footage, everything gets transcribed, embedded, described, and face-detected. You can scrub your footage locally after you drag it in, but we upload a low-res proxy so your teammates and cloud inference can see it. This local scrubbing plus custom pro media decoders means you can drag a 250GB ProRes clip from your new iPhone right into your Kino timeline. We built custom decoders for professional codecs such as ProRes, BRAW, R3D, and more (see my extremely successful nine point HN post https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50198052). None of the performance we’re getting would have been possible before WebCodecs and libraries like Mediabunny.

I grew up making YouTube videos, and during my undergrad at MIT I co-directed a 3.5 hour archival footage documentary on the history of my school and technological development in America (https://regressions.net). Much of the work was logging footage, managing hard drives, manually syncing Premiere project state, and planning our movie in a spreadsheet.

Our first launch in 2023 proclaimed that Kino was "Silicon Valley meets Hollywood." It was more like Palantir for Hollywood; we ran bespoke on-prem Kino deployments with our team of forward deployed engineers on shows like Survivor and A24's Beef. It was a rush, but it felt like the slowest way to improve video editing for the whole world. Bound by the Avid Media Composer and strict studio security rules, we couldn't touch frontier models, and we couldn't make editors >10x faster. So in 2025, we rebuilt Kino as a true editor, and we took a bet on coding-as-editing.

Everything in Kino has a URL: projects, clips, footage, comments and replies, even a single frame and the line of code that draws it. Projects and media living in one place and everything being addressable means that your agents and team have a single, editable source of truth for video production. At a lower level, I now paste Kino links into my agent constantly, whether it’s making sure Codex knows exactly which timeline item (among thousands) I am referring to or which teammate’s comment needs fixing.

We have teams managing their whole company’s media in Kino, spinning up agents to make new videos every day, then using review links to flag issues. One founder ships ads like this: each day he uses Kino's YouTube support to find b-roll he is allowed to use, he edits something, his co-founder leaves notes such as “we need to use this clip instead” and his agent can then apply them. Full-time filmmakers are also using Kino. They tend to resemble “toxenmaxxer” software developers, where 15+ agents iterate on a single project, each trusting Kino as the source of truth for timeline state, graphics, media, everything.

The full editor is free, including unlimited imports and exports, real-time collaboration and MCP access for your own agent. Pro is $25 per editor per month and adds unlimited MCP tool calls, share links, more storage, YouTube search, and the ability to edit alongside your team. You can download it at https://kino.ai. We have not yet released Kino for the pure web browser, just Electron for now.

If you make videos personally, if you have ProRes media and you want to try to break Kino, if you have legacy video editor projects to bring in, or if you want to make more content for your company, we'd love to hear how Kino works for you.

items.title: This might sound weird coming from a "guy making content" because I should sell you difficult setups, but the best Claud
items.content:
This might sound weird coming from a "guy making content" because I should sell you difficult setups, but the best Claude setup is no setup:

Let's start with-

> Not using Claude with a personal account.
> Not using Claude without its desktop app.
> Not using Claude without trying Claude Code.

Then the actual setup of your Claude:

(mind you, delete this setup again in 5 months)

1. Check that you have one Claude.

Go to Claude Settings → Organization Settings → Capabilities.

2. Pick 'Auto' in Claude Chat.

In the message box, switch Manual to Auto. Claude works without stopping to ask you at every step.

Default: Opus 5.5 + High + Auto.

3. Claude Chat writes code.

Everything is code. A slide. An image. A video. 

So when Claude can write code, it builds the thing instead of describing it.

Now, go to the left menu bar in Claude. Pick Design.

Pick Slides. Write a prompt of what you want exactly. Prompt it until you like what you see. You can upload references too.

4. Delete your old Claude setup.

> Account → “Instructions for Claude." Empty.
> Claude Customize → Skills. Remove.
> Skills → Yours → Search “writing” → Turn off.
> Claude Settings → Memory → Turn it off.
> Any over-organised folder you maintain.
> Delete global instructions. It ignores it anyway.

5. One clear goal.

Prompting is sharing your goal. Claude figures out the how. It can’t guess what you want (and why).

Start all the new chats with this prompt template:

"Goal: [what you want, and what it's for] Context: [who it's for, what you already have, what good looks like] Before you start, restate in your own words what you think my goals are and the problem I'm trying to solve. If you need more context, ask me questions."

6. Ask for HTML page.

Stop asking for a Word file, a PowerPoint or a PDF. 

Try asking for an HTML. Claude builds it as an Artifact: a web page that lives in your Claude account. 

Add this to your prompt:

"Make it an HTML page."

7. Switch from your old folders.

Open the Claude desktop app & select your old folder (mine was called CLAUDE COWORK). It’s the last time Claude reads it.

I wrote a prompt to clean my folder aggressively. LinkedIn limited me from sharing that long prompt because of the character limit. But to copy the prompt (for free), go to https://t.co/NYWCbdGAVl

I will make this post again in the next 5 months to make you delete your (then) old setup and start from scratch.

Even Anthropic’s team is doing it:

“Every 6 months, delete your Claude MD. Delete your skills. Delete your hooks. See what the model does, and it might surprise you.” 

- Boris Cherny (the guy who built Claude code)

Stop sending Claude-slop to your boss.
It's putting you on the edge of getting fired.
I am sure you're (definitely) sending a report with:

> unnecessary wall of text.
> titles/headings that sound like poetry.
> 12 cluttered boxes, and no idea where to start.
> no clue what you yourself are looking at, and why.

I like how Shopify's CEO calls it "slop grenades."

I spent an entire day figuring out how to un-slop those reports, whether you are the one sending or receiving them.

Here's how:

Step 1. Copy the prompt from my guide: https://t.co/4GBb1RcBDp

It has my free GitHub repo link. No, it's not technical

→ If you're making a new report
Copy the "make a page" prompt from the guide.

→ If you are fixing an existing one
Copy the "fix a page" prompt from the same guide.

Step 2. Attach your AI slop report to Claude.

> Your meeting notes.
> Your spreadsheet.
> Your existing report.
> Or an overwhelmingly slopped page someone just sent you to do the job, they are supposed to.

Step 3. Tell Claude (specifically) WHO will read it.

Your prompt "For Dana, my colleague" is a NO-go
Be painfully specific like: "For Dana, my CFO".
Then tell it what Dana needs to do after reading.

Step 4. The report needs to only have ONE job.

→ Either to make a decision? Put the ask on top.
→ Or to catch up? Lead with 3 or 4 numbers.
→ Or to learn a process? One step per screen.
→ Or to approve a proposal? One idea per slide.

Step 5. Now, go back to Step 1 and paste the prompt from the guide.

Do not ignore that prompt, it is going to un-slop by Claude reading my rules, then building the page for your reader.

Don't worry. You install nothing.

The prompts, before-and-after examples, and 7 types of pages are here:

https://t.co/4GBb1RcBDp

Take the last report you sent. Fix that one first.

items.content:
It's hard to believe that an AI freak like me uses less AI than ever before. Here are the only 4 apps I open (every day):

> Claude (and Claude Code)
> Slack, to talk to my team
> Wispr Flow, for meeting notes & voice dictation
> Viktor, our AI employee in Slack

Viktor is on the list because he fixes the one thing that annoyed me about Claude:

Claude is only between me and the AI. I can’t bring/loop my team into the conversation.

As crazy as it sounds, I officially hired Viktor and added him to my team Slack. 

Now my team & I talk to each other in Slack, and Viktor collaborates with the entire team, using both Anisha’s Claude and mine (+ connected to all our apps).

Here’s what that looked like (watch the video):

1. I asked Anisha to turn my latest newsletter, “Claude for legal,” into a LinkedIn post.
2. Anisha sent a Slack message tagging @Viktor to build a page in Claude Code with prompts from the article.
3. Viktor replied with a live page link (in 2 mins).
4. I jumped in: I think we should do it differently.
5. Viktor started working with both of us in thread.
6. He went to my Substack, pulled the content, and built a lead magnet. Replied “Done” with a link.

This is what I wanted out of Claude Tag, a proactive collaboration. But it has too many bugs, so I hired Viktor instead.

How to set it up for your team:

1. Go to viktor .com & add it to your Slack (works in Microsoft Teams too).
2. Connect the tools you want it to use. I added the Claude API, for him to build in Claude Code.
3. Tag @Viktor in a channel with any task, written the way you’d message a team member.
4. Correct it in the thread when something’s off.

Instead of endlessly tweaking prompts or relying on generic models, you describe what you want your agent to accomplish, and FAiE handles the engineering behind it.

It designs evaluations, finds failures, curates training data, chooses strategies, and runs experiments.

Just 15 minutes of your input. A few hours of automated AI engineering.

Moving from prompting AI agents to actually training them could be a much bigger shift than it sounds. 🚀

She leans over at the bar and says, "So YOU have a million subscribers? But why do they read YOU?"

She's right. I am no
items.content:
She leans over at the bar and says, "So YOU have a million subscribers? But why do they read YOU?"

She's right. I am not gifted.
I am simply:

Obsessed over useful + practical AI.
Curious about how to best teach humans.
Chronically online (so you, my audience, aren't).
Against AI hype news (so I can focus on 'how').
Willing to write twice a week, no matter what.
Optimistic about technology. I reject doomerism.
A risk taker. I might be wrong, but I'll try anyway.
A French guy living in Tel Aviv writing in English?
Someone who doesn't know how to code (at all).
Dying to know how the world will evolve with AI.
Never stopping until everyone masters AI easily.
On a mission: AI isn't hard & can make us better.
A 29-year-old with no tricks or secrets to sell.
Happy to go to work. Major advantage in life.
Working 6 days a week, 9-to-6, no cold plunge.
Keeping my computer at the office. Never home.
Paying for most AI + testing them (so you don't).
Not thinking of '1 million' but rather '1 person'.

So that's how I ended up with 1 million email subscribers on Substack on 'How to AI'.

I can hear some of you saying, "Why a newsletter? No one reads. Go on YouTube."

And they are also right! YouTube has 100x the audience of Substack or any newsletter.

But I am focused on education. And I found my format to best teach my testings & learnings.

Because I don't learn much from YouTube. I personally read more. So I thought, "maybe others do too, I will write for them".

I never thought a million of you would.

I can't really wrap my head around the number "1 million" (I mean Tel Aviv, where I live, has 400,000 inhabitants?? it can't be).

But I am very grateful to each and every one of you.

I wrote "Master AI before it masters you" on December 7, 2022, a week after ChatGPT came out.

I was both so afraid and so excited about the technology of "LLMs": they could talk like us, think like us, and give us superhuman powers the same way electricity or fire did.

I don't know how to end this post. I rarely celebrate or show my face. I think teaching is more interesting than storytelling. And I won't shamelessly plug my newsletter (sorry for my team, I know it's tempting).

Maybe I can end it by answering the girl at the bar?

It really happened, and I probably babbled, "Aha! I don't know. Anyway..."

But if I could switch answers, I'd say: "You are right. I am not gifted. Maybe you should write one too!"

items.title:
"We basically ended up vibe coding a bunch of slop."

This is what a co-founder of a company that builds software for go
items.content:
"We basically ended up vibe coding a bunch of slop."

This is what a co-founder of a company that builds software for government agencies told our team.

Under their earlier technical leadership, the team built with a spec-driven AI tool. On paper they did everything right. Specs first, agents building from the specs, tests generated automatically.

Their two senior engineers walked us through what they found when they looked closer.

The specs were written by AI too. "The specs themselves were vibe coded and not properly curated by a human." So the system design decisions inside them went straight into the code. The tool also left piles of generated documents in the repo, and the engineers now plan to delete most of them.

The agent said it was done when it wasn't. "The agent says, yeah, I did the thing, and it didn't do the thing."

The tests passed every time. They were "testing the same thing that's in the code," so they could never fail.

Every check in that process was AI checking AI.

When our team showed them delivery dashboards with commits shipped and tickets closed, their engineers pushed back. "It's not a quality measurement." The co-founder wanted to know how we avoid hallucination, context rot and poor abstraction. Fair question.

The reality is the spec is the one part you can't hand to the model. Here's how our engineers answered it:

> audit the codebase before anyone builds, so you know what the slop already broke
> a person writes and signs off every spec, and the agent only helps draft it
> the spec gets a changelog in the pipeline, so it still matches the feature after the tenth change
> tests come from the spec, never from the code they're testing
> each module gets a short context file, so the agent stops guessing what it is

Then the pilot they asked for. One feature from their customer backlog, not trivial, judged on speed, quality and cost before anything bigger.

AI is an amplifier.

Give it specs nobody read and it amplifies the bullshit.

items.title:
Ontology, Knowledge Graphs, and the Decision Model That Judges Them

Building knowledge graphs with LLMs has a cost stru
items.content:
Ontology, Knowledge Graphs, and the Decision Model That Judges Them

Building knowledge graphs with LLMs has a cost structure that is easy to misread. Extraction is cheap and getting cheaper. Verification is where the money goes.

For every candidate entity and every candidate relation, something has to decide whether it is true to the document. That judgment repeats tens of thousands of times, which is the job a decision model exists for. 

The model in question is Jev, a small decision model from TypeSafe built to take a claim, weigh the evidence and commit to an answer.

The pattern it challenges:
- One large model handling extraction, summarisation and community building, with every step billed at frontier rates
-The model that proposes a fact also being the one that grades it
-Reasoning models adding a deliberation meter, paying for pages of thinking to collect one-word yes/no verdicts

OntoSmith splits the work into three layers:
-A cheap mid-tier model proposes triples (Claude Haiku 5.5 in the reference setup). It reads and suggests. It does not decide.
-A fitted pair call and then Jev judge every candidate before anything reaches the graph
-A frontier model is reserved for the genuinely hard calls

The shared map is the ontology: versioned, hash-pinned packs for open-domain text, legal contracts and biomedical literature over a domain-neutral core. For a document type with no ready ontology, one is drafted for approval. The graph lives in Neo4j, one graph per ontology build.

This is not RAG versus Graph RAG. Search handles answers that sit in one paragraph. Graphs add value when relations span pages: +0.080 recall@20 (0.631 to 0.712) on a pinned 116-question set over long contracts, and exactly zero on short abstracts.

The measured figures:
-3.8 cents per document across 500 documents in the flagship build
-About 7 cents per document projected for judging alone in the default configuration
-Corrected graph precision of 0.911 [0.892 to 0.928], revised down after a re-audit by a judge from a different model family, with the working shipped alongside

One lesson from the build: a decision model on default parameters is someone else’s operating point. Thresholds were fitted stage by stage, and experiments that missed their pre-registered bars stayed in the record as failures.

OntoSmith is MIT-licensed, on PyPI (pip install ontosmith) and on GitHub. 🔎

Take this as feedback from someone who maintains three Claude Ultra accounts exclusively for game development.

The issu
items.content:
Take this as feedback from someone who maintains three Claude Ultra accounts exclusively for game development.

The issue is that basically everything in game development is derivative to some degree, whether that's controls, mechanics, objectives, themes, genres, or established design conventions. So telling developers to simply "build something original" borders on being deliberately misleading - particularly when Claude is already notoriously risk averse and inclined to interpret ambiguity as licence to disregard explicit instructions, produce an inferior result because it substituted its own judgement for the developer's, or simply refuse outright and meander around the request.

From my perspective there are two separate issues here:

1) What is legally permissible and...
2) What is Anthropic choosing to prohibit through model policy.

Conflating the two and not defining it only makes this discussion more frustrating.

From a legal standpoint, creating a spiritual successor or drawing inspiration from existing games is legal. This is not debatable. Copyright protects particular expressions of ideas, not broad concepts, genres, or gameplay mechanics in the abstract. Obviously, there is nuance to this, like the involvement of protected assets, distinctive expression, trademarks, and other intellectual property rights... but those are separate legal considerations. They don't suddenly make the concept of developing a game inspired by an existing title illegal.

For what it's worth, Anthropic is entitled to establish whatever restrictions it wants for Claude. It's a free market after all... but there's a clear fucking difference between product and policy decisions, and the actual law, and they should be defended on their own merits rather than disingenuously presented as though it's not one but the other when it's clearly not. Which everyone basically is calling you out for.

I, and I think many others, have basically zero issue with Claude as a service denying its users the ability to decrypt or unpack game assets to then go on to clone into a new game or steal...

But "make me Mario Kart, except with dinosaurs" should be an entirely legitimate request. And until this change after you guys introduced all this shit... it wasn't. Which is outlandishly fucking stupid.

Taking an established concept and reimagining it with different mechanics, characters, environments, or themes is practically the foundation of game development. Inspiration is not infringement, and a model policy that treats the two as interchangeable is restrictive for no good reason.

And even with the updated approach, which is supposedly more UX-friendly, the underlying problem remains. The moment Claude starts independently interpreting the broader context to determine whether a game is sufficiently "original," you're introducing another subjective layer into its reasoning. That creates opportunities for false positives, unnecessary refusals, and degraded output quality. Instead of executing the developer's instructions, the model risks substituting its own creative and policy judgements for what the developer actually requested.

What makes this especially mind boggling to me is the inconsistency across your platform. Users can instruct Claude to build a "clone of X, Y, or Z SaaS product," replicate established application workflows/modalities or recreate the functionality of competing software basically 1:1, and it'll happily get to work until every but the logo is different. Yet suddenly game development warrants this extraordinary level of scrutiny?

I genuinely don't understand Anthropic's position here. Your post has done nothing to clarify anything. Claude Code had finally reached a point where we genuinely have frontier-class intelligence game development, and rather than capitalising on that, you've introduced friction into one of its most promising use cases.

For what, exactly? Is this addressing a demonstrable legal risk, a specific pattern of actual abuse, or simply Anthropic's preferred philosophy about what constitutes sufficiently original creative work?

Because these are all three very different things, and your customers deserve to know which one is driving a policy that can materially affect the quality and reliability of the product they're paying for.

how to get claude code to listen to 500 industry podcasts for you and hand you a warm B2B buyer list every morning

your
items.content:
how to get claude code to listen to 500 industry podcasts for you and hand you a warm B2B buyer list every morning

your next $20,000 client just spent 45 minutes explaining the exact problem they need you to fix

they said it 34 minutes into a niche podcast that only got 80 views on youtube

a CEO who deletes 120 sales emails a week will go on a small trade podcast and confess every broken part of his business to the host because he forgets anyone outside his industry is listening

we run outbound for B2B companies

if you point an AI pipeline at those transcripts, you get a daily list of founders telling you what they want to buy in their own words

any operator can build their own version of this in an afternoon

what you are training the agent to catch

when a founder goes on a podcast, he never talks like a press release

- a logistics VP admits their current software breaks every time they add a new warehouse
- a healthcare group owner mentions they are losing nurses because their scheduling is still on spreadsheets
- a SaaS CEO complains that their paid ads stalled in Q3 and their sales reps have empty calendars

none of those problems ever show up on apollo or linkedin job boards

when your agent pulls the 90-second clip where the founder said it, you have who said it, the timestamp, the exact words he used, and the company he runs

nobody on your team has to listen to a single minute of audio

how to build one

1. build the show list. podscan tracks millions of podcasts and carries the full transcripts, or you can use apify to pull transcripts straight off youtube channels in your market. skip the famous business shows and pull 300 to 500 tiny niche shows where your buyers get interviewed as guests, like "the modern freight podcast" or "dental group leaders". judge the show by the guests in the title, never by the view count.

2. write the context file (claude .md). this is the whole trick. yours should hold who you sell to, the deal math, your best past openers, and a written disqualifier list. if you are chasing a specific problem this month, put it in the file so the agent hunts for it across every new episode.

3. split the reading across two models. every morning, pull the transcripts of any episode published in the last 24 hours. don't use keyword filters because the best buying signals are passing remarks in the middle of a story about something else. have a cheap model like gemini (using the $300 free API credits) or sonnet read the full transcripts first to flag any guest who mentioned a bottleneck. then have claude opus read only the flagged passages to verify if the guest fits your ICP.

4. cross-reference the guest and send the message. once opus flags a guest, have a second agent find their linkedin profile and verified email through blitz API and mailtester ninja.

never tell the founder "i heard you on a podcast at minute 34" because that sounds like a stalker

use the exact internal vocabulary they used on the show in a two-line message:

- subject line: their first name
- line 1: "hey mark, we just helped a [their industry] firm fix [exact problem they mentioned on the show] and got them [one client result] in 30 days"
- line 2: "worth a look if that's on your radar for Q4?"

what goes wrong if you build it badly

if you try to put the scraping, the qualification, and the copywriting inside one giant prompt, the model gets lazy and starts hallucinating problems the guest never said

split it into three separate agents where each one has one job:

- agent 1 only pulls the passage and the timestamp from the transcript
- agent 2 checks the guest's company against your disqualifier list and writes down one sentence on why they passed or failed
- agent 3 writes four variations of the two-line message and runs them through a spam test before you ever see the draft

auto-generated transcripts also mess up company names and swap what the host said with what the guest said

forcing the second read to quote the speaker word-for-word with the timestamp kills 90% of the bad sends

everyone is looking for something useful to do with AI besides writing generic blog posts

start by writing one page about your best customer and the 5 problems you solve, then point claude at the shows your buyers talk on

في الجزء الأول غطّينا أساسيات الـ Claude Agent SDK، وشرحنا الفرق بينه وبين الـ frameworks التانية، وبنينا وشغّلنا أول agentic loop.

GitHub is hiding some INSANE tools for making money with AI.

I found 10 open-source repos that can help you turn an idea into a real business.

From building products to finding customers.

Here they are:

1. Saasfly

Start your SaaS with authentication, payments, a database, and reusable UI components. Give Claude Code or Codex a foundation to build on.

https://t.co/t7haHyYJfb

2. R2R

Turn business documents into searchable AI knowledge bases. Build specialized research assistants and tools that answer questions about company data.

https://t.co/m45OWcQUbd

3. Scira

An AI search engine that finds information and cites its sources. Research competitors or use it as a starting point for a niche search product.

https://t.co/X3ZbiVZfyP

4. Lago

Add usage-based billing to your AI product. Track tokens, API calls, or other usage, then turn that activity into subscriptions and invoices.

https://t.co/ppghC3L5c7

5. Marketing Skills

Give your AI coding assistant reusable workflows for SEO, keyword research, content strategy, paid ads, and product launches.

https://t.co/shdrRZyhJw

6. Google Maps Scraper

Find potential customers by collecting business names, websites, phone numbers, and reviews. Optional email extraction checks their websites for contact details.

https://t.co/DcCqLg0kWj

7. Frappe CRM

Keep your leads, deals, notes, and follow-up tasks in one place. Track sales conversations with a visual drag-and-drop pipeline.

https://t.co/1600DjoIDB

8. Dittofeed

Build automated onboarding emails, customer follow-ups, and marketing campaigns. Trigger messages based on what users actually do.

https://t.co/KQwmGqRNQn

9. Papermark

Share proposals, sales decks, and documents through branded links with built-in tracking. Useful for pitching AI services and landing clients.

https://t.co/DWPQVH16Oz

10. Counterscale

Run your own website analytics on Cloudflare. Track pageviews and referral sources to see where your landing-page traffic comes from.

https://t.co/JHRbP9EebI

Open-source code doesn’t mean zero running costs. Hosting, AI APIs, and other services can cost extra.

items.content:
“I can't grow my business because I don't have any influencers”

A SaaS founder on Reddit got quoted $10K for one post.
The influencer has 1M followers and mostly reviews general tech.

Then another brand asked an agency and got quoted $4K for 1 reel and 1 story.
The agency's creators have 40K-150K followers, and their stories get 1K-12K views.

Then a marketer said small creators are asking $1K+ per video.
And some of them can't even write a decent script.

One of the biggest limiting beliefs is that you ‘can't grow without influencers.’

The uncomfortable truth is that you don't need someone else's face to sell your product.

You can build your own without filming a thing

Just go to AvatarFactory:

Step 1: Connect AvatarFactory to Claude
Open Claude's Settings, go to Connectors, and click Add custom connector. Paste the AvatarFactory MCP URL, sign in, and approve it. If you don't have a plan yet, it'll ask you to start the $1 trial first. On Claude Code, it's one add command in the terminal. After that, the AvatarFactory tools show up in every chat.

Step 2: Ask Claude what's working in your niche
Tell Claude your niche and ask what's trending. It runs the trend tool, which draws on more than 50 million analyzed reels, and gives you the hooks, formats, and angles taking off right now. A regular Claude chat can't do this, because on its own it has no idea what the feed rewarded this week.

Step 3: Shape the persona
Ask Claude to turn your niche into a full AI influencer concept. It drafts the face, the voice, and the point of view. Push back, refine it, and lock in the version you like. The persona is what you're really building, so spend a minute here. The same character is going to front every video you make.

Step 4: Build the avatar
Claude sends you to the AvatarFactory app, where you build a face and voice for your persona that stay the same in every reel. The avatar comes first, because the script tool writes in a saved avatar's voice. Already built one? Claude can pull up your saved avatars and pick the right one.

Step 5: Write the reel script
Back in Claude, ask for a reel in your persona's voice. It writes the script from the trend an open-loop hook in the first second, a reason to keep watching, a payoff worth saving, and the call to action at the end. Read it, tweak a line, and approve it. Scripts come out of your plan allowance, and Claude sends back a render link with your avatar already selected.

Step 6: Render the video
Hit render in the app. AvatarFactory makes a captioned vertical video in about 3 minutes and uses your credits like any other render. 

Download the MP4 and post it to Reels, TikTok, and Shorts.

Done.
